name: french yogurt cake
instructions:
1 CUP OF FAT TOTAL is the load-bearing requirement (see notes on the fat structure). Two ways to hit it:

STANDARD (ALL-YOGURT PATH): ratio 3:2:1:1 (flour:sugar:yogurt:oil) where 1 part = 1/2 cup. So 1.5 cup all-purpose flour (not wheat or cake), 1 cup sugar, 1/2 cup yogurt, 1/2 cup oil = 1 cup fat total. Plus 3 eggs, 2 tsp baking powder, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tsp vanilla. Bake at 350.

BUTTER VARIANT: 1/4 cup yogurt + 1/4 cup butter (in place of the standard yogurt/oil split). CUT BAKING POWDER TO 1.5 tsp (from 2 tsp) when using butter. Otherwise same as above.
notes:
=== 1 CUP OF FAT TOTAL — THE LOAD-BEARING REQUIREMENT ===

The cake needs 1 cup of fat total. The standard 3:2:1:1 ratio hits this via 1/2 cup oil + 1/2 cup yogurt. That's the canonical path.

BUTTER VARIANT: 1/4 cup yogurt + 1/4 cup butter also works as an alternative to the standard yogurt half. When using butter, CUT BAKING POWDER FROM 2 tsp TO 1.5 tsp — the butter changes the leavening math and the full amount is too much. For the pure-yogurt version keep the full 2 tsp.

PLAIN YOGURT TENDS TO DO BETTER THAN GREEK — BOTH WORK: plain yogurt is the preferred choice. Greek yogurt is strained (thicker, higher protein, lower water), and in this recipe that translates to a drier, denser crumb — the cake depends on the yogurt for moisture as much as for tang. Plain yogurt's higher water content gives you the softer, more tender result the dish wants. Greek still works in a pinch; just expect a slightly denser cake. If using greek, a small splash of milk or water can help compensate for the missing moisture.

vegetable or olive oil both acceptable.

=== ALMONDS AND WALNUTS ARE BOTH GREAT IN THE BATTER ===

Both almonds and walnuts work in the batter. Almonds are the more common pick; walnuts add a slightly more earthy/richer character. Either or both is fine — nut ballast is what the all-purpose-flour base depends on structurally (see MAY 9 experiment notes below).

WHY NUTS WORK HERE BUT NOT IN THE GREEK YOGURT POUND CAKE: this cake's bread-like sturdier crumb can suspend nuts. The greek-yogurt-lemon-pound-cake sibling has a fluffier/softer crumb (my observation) and comes out better without any nuts inside — the crumb can't hold them. Opposite guidance across the two.

=== IT NEEDS FROSTING — STURDY BUTTERCREAM OR WHITE CHOCOLATE FUDGE ===

This cake wants a frosting; it's not a bare-cake dessert. Top choices:
- STURDY BUTTERCREAM FROSTING: vanilla buttercream is the classic pairing — clean sweet dairy that complements the cake's lemon-and-yogurt tang without competing. Use the sturdy thick style (butter or crisco based); the bread-like crumb can carry it.
- WHITE CHOCOLATE FUDGE: also works as a topping. Similar sturdy-sweet-dairy register as the buttercream.

CHOCOLATE FROSTING PROBABLY OK, DARK CHOCOLATE IS A CONFIRMED MISTAKE: regular (milk) chocolate frosting is probably fine — untested but reasonable. DARK CHOCOLATE frosting was a huge mistake in a past attempt — the bitterness fought the lemon-and-yogurt cake register. Skip dark chocolate.

IF YOU MAKE A THICK BUTTER/CRISCO-STYLE FROSTING (rather than a lighter icing): scatter pepitas (pumpkin seeds) on top for extra protein. Adds a nutty crunch against the dense sweet frosting and offsets some of the sugar density with real substance.

WHY FROSTING NOT COMPOTE HERE: the bread-like sturdier crumb wants a sturdy sweet topping that sits on it. The greek-yogurt-lemon-pound-cake sibling gets the opposite guidance — that fluffier cake is better with a compote on top than a frosting. Opposite guidance across the two.

=== FAILURE — LEMON JUICE IN THE CAKE OR FROSTING ===

Lemon JUICE (not zest) is a failure in both the cake batter and the frosting. Zest is fine and encouraged; juice adds water and a different kind of acidity that reads as sour rather than bright. Same rule as elsewhere in the cookbook — when a recipe wants 'lemon,' it usually wants zest.

=== FRUIT COMPOTE / ICING IS DEFINITIVELY SUBOPTIMAL HERE — REACH FOR FROSTING INSTEAD ===

Hardened stance: fruit compote (strawberry, blueberry, or otherwise) is DEFINITIVELY SUBOPTIMAL on this cake. Reach for the sturdy buttercream / white chocolate fudge / regular chocolate options in the FROSTING section above instead. The bread-like sturdier crumb here wants a sturdy sweet topping, not a fruit sauce.

Where compote DOES belong: the greek-yogurt-lemon-pound-cake sibling. That cake is fluffier and compote lands correctly there (with its own visual-aging caveat — see that recipe).

HISTORICAL NOTE ON SEEPING BEHAVIOR: earlier notes here described the fruit topping slowly seeping into the cake over the days after assembly, and framed this as a feature (day 1 vs day 2 vs day 3 flavor evolution). The flavor aging is real. The visual isn't — strawberry compote in particular looks like blood-and-guts by the next day and reads unpresentable to other people. Blueberry ages more gracefully visually. But the underlying stance is: skip the compote here regardless. It's suboptimal.

=== SUCCESSFUL SPICE EXPERIMENTS — CINNAMON AND GARAM MASALA (SKIP NUTMEG) ===

Cinnamon and garam masala both add a lot to this cake. Both are welcome. Nutmeg specifically doesn't work here — skip it.

AUG 13 2026 EXPERIMENT (chocolate variant with natural cocoa): skipped the lemon peel and swapped 1/4 cup of flour for 1/4 cup of NATURAL cocoa powder.

Result — didn't turn out well:
- Fruity/funky flavor. Attribute this to using natural cocoa powder instead of cacao powder (or dutched cocoa).
- Spongey and flat texture. This texture works for the lemon version of the cake, but chocolate cakes should be fluffier and less tangy.

Lesson: the base french yogurt cake recipe is tuned for a lemon-forward register. Turning it into a chocolate cake needs more than a flour-for-cocoa swap — the tangy-and-spongey character that suits lemon fights chocolate. If retrying the chocolate direction, use cacao or dutched cocoa (not natural), and probably needs recipe-level adjustments beyond the flour swap to get the fluffier-and-less-tangy chocolate cake register.

MAY 9 2026 EXPERIMENT (strawberry-jam variant): tried two changes at once. (1) Reduced sugar slightly and folded strawberry jam into the batter. (2) Moved the almonds out of the batter and onto the top of the frosting (sliced/slivered).

Results — bad:
- Cake came out WAY sweeter than intended despite the sugar reduction. Possible explanation: the jam may have had corn syrup, which compensated for the sugar cut and then some. Worth checking the jam label next time.
- Cake was also fluffier than normal. Some of that is good — this recipe uses all-purpose flour rather than cake flour, and the extra gluten usually makes it tough. But the fluffiness combined with the sweetness made it cloying.
- Got a tummy ache after just a few bites. The combination of more sweetness + softer crumb + jam-spiked frosting was too much sugar density.
- Removing the almonds from the batter compounded the texture issue. When almonds get mashed into the batter they contribute literal almond flour, which adds structure and offsets the all-purpose-flour-too-soft-but-also-too-glutenous problem. Pulling them out lost that ballast.
- The cream cheese frosting had strawberry jam mixed in (made it pink and flavorful, which was nice visually) but it was also too sweet — same corn-syrup-jam suspicion.

Lessons for next attempt: keep the almonds IN the batter; if using jam, use a low-sugar / no-corn-syrup variety, or reduce the sugar more aggressively to compensate; consider whether to skip the jam entirely and use lemon zest instead to keep the cake closer to its canonical balance.

CLAUDE'S THOUGHTS (on the may 9 experiment):

- The corn-syrup hypothesis is probably not the main culprit. Even sugar-only strawberry jams are 50-60% sugar by weight, so 1/3-1/2 cup of jam carries 30-60g of added sugar — substantially more than a 'slight sugar reduction' offsets. Jam also concentrates sweetness perception via low water activity and pectin gel; the same grams read sweeter in baked form than crystalline sugar would. Most likely the jam's sugar load was just under-counted. Diagnostic for next time: read the nutrition label and subtract grams-of-sugar-per-spoonful from the cake's sugar quantity 1:1.

- Both changes pulled fluffiness in the same direction. Jam is ~30-40% water; folding it in dilutes the batter and suppresses gluten formation. Removing almonds removed real structural ballast (almond flour, fat, protein) — when almonds get partially mashed during mixing, they contribute almond-flour-like behavior that this all-purpose-flour recipe specifically depends on. Net: more moisture + less ballast = a softer crumb that also dissolves faster on the palate, which makes the sugar hit harder. The tummy ache probably tracks both the sugar density AND the rapid digestion of the soft crumb.

- Suggestions for the next attempt:
  1. Keep almonds IN the batter. The intuition there is right.
  2. For strawberry flavor, consider non-jam sources: freeze-dried strawberry powder (real flavor, no water, no sugar) or homemade unsweetened strawberry purée. These let the strawberry-flavor knob and the sugar-and-moisture knob be tuned separately.
  3. For the toughness problem at the structural level, consider substituting ~1/3 of the all-purpose with cake flour. Reduces gluten without adding water — hits the tenderness target intentionally rather than via accidental moisture.
  4. For the frosting, lemon-zested cream cheese frosting plus fresh sliced strawberries as garnish. Skips the jam-on-jam sugar stacking; lemon zest gives the cake a brighter acid frame.

=== SIBLING RECIPE — GREEK YOGURT LEMON POUND CAKE ===

Different cake, easy to confuse: greek-yogurt-lemon-pound-cake is a POUND cake (loaf format) built on greek yogurt (specifically), cold butter (not oil), lemon-sugar-rub technique, cold-oven start, and baking powder PLUS baking soda. Walks the line between sweet and savory per its source.

ACTUAL TEXTURE COMPARISON: despite the pound-cake format LOOKING like it should be denser, my observation is that the greek yogurt cake comes out noticeably fluffier and more cake-like, and THIS french yogurt cake reads more bread-like. See the greek-yogurt-lemon-pound-cake IN PRACTICE note for details.

OPPOSITE SERVING GUIDANCE ACROSS THE TWO:
- THIS CAKE (french-yogurt-cake, bread-like): nuts INSIDE welcome (crumb sturdy enough to suspend them); topped with sturdy buttercream or white chocolate fudge. Compote is definitively suboptimal here.
- GREEK YOGURT POUND CAKE (fluffier): NO nuts inside (crumb can't suspend them); compote works (make and serve immediately — visual ages poorly), whipped cream or ice cream also work.

See that recipe for the full comparison across eight axes.
why_i_like_this_recipe: Best pantry cake (nothing unusual like cocoa powder, or cake flour, or espresso). Can be made versatile with a fruit topping / tastes different every time. Can be made very high protein with 3 eggs + greek yogurt to 1 cup of sugar, and can be overloaded with nuts and seeds to very little detrimental effects (better protein ratios than many sweets, at least).
